routes.description: Establish that necessary truths are propositions requiring an ontological ground, that propositions are intrinsically intentional and best understood as thoughts, and that their objectivity and necessity require an eternal divine mind rather than human minds or mind-independent abstract objects.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by securing proposition realism, connecting propositional intentionality to mentality, showing that a necessary divine mind can ground objective and necessary propositions, and establishing an explanatory advantage over Platonism and other alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Connect the existence and character of necessary propositions to their grounding as thoughts in a necessarily existing divine mind.

centralBridges.description: Establish that necessary truths involve real propositions rather than merely linguistic, physical, or human constructions.
Show that the intrinsic aboutness and aspectual character of propositions are best explained by treating propositions as thoughts.
Show that divine thoughts can supply propositions with necessary existence, objectivity, and shareability without depending on contingent human cognition.
Demonstrate that divine conceptualism explains intentionality and causal relevance more fully than mind-independent Platonism.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Identify at least one unavoidable truth without requiring certainty about any particular classical logical law or a complete theory of modality.
Explain how divine thoughts can constitute propositional contents without generating a distinctive content regress or self-reference problem.

routes.description: Establish that necessary propositions can exist objectively without being divine thoughts, that intentionality does not entail mentality, and that Platonist realism accounts for necessity, shared content, and mathematical discovery without requiring a necessarily existing divine mind.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by granting or independently supporting necessary propositions while blocking the inference from propositions to thoughts, exposing coherence or explanatory problems in divine conceptualism, and presenting a viable non-theistic realist account.

motionBridge.description: Show that necessary propositions admit a coherent non-divine explanation, so their existence does not require a necessarily existing divine mind.

centralBridges.description: Establish that propositions may possess intentionality without being mental and that the contrary inference needs independent support.
Show that mind-independent propositions can account for objective, shareable, and necessarily true contents.
Test whether identifying propositions with divine thoughts yields determinate content without regress, relabeling, or an unstable thought-content distinction.
Show that divine conceptualism does not gain an explanatory or ontological advantage merely by redescribing abstract propositions as divine thoughts.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish logical, epistemic, and metaphysical necessity and require adequate support for claims about unavoidable truths.
Separate objections common to proposition realism from considerations that genuinely discriminate between divine conceptualism and Platonism.

sections.title: Necessary truths and the operative modality
sections.rationale: This issue determines the argument's starting point, including whether some truth could not have been false and how disputes over particular logical laws or possible-world restrictions affect that commitment.

sections.title: Reality, objectivity, and shareability of propositions
sections.rationale: The competing accounts require a common ontology of truth-bearers, making arguments from communication, discovery, translation, and undiscovered truths structurally important.

sections.title: Whether propositional intentionality requires mentality
sections.rationale: This is the principal bridge from necessary propositions to thoughts and therefore from necessary truth to a mind, while the opposing route requires a nonmental account of aboutness and content.

sections.title: Coherence of divine thoughts as propositional contents
sections.rationale: The divine account must explain how thoughts can constitute objective contents without regress or equivocation, while the critique must show why the proposed divine cognition cannot fill that role.

sections.title: Divine conceptualism and Platonism compared
sections.rationale: The motion ultimately turns on whether a divine mind is needed once both views address necessity, intentionality, causal relevance, parsimony, mathematical discovery, and liabilities shared by realist theories.
